The exercise is onesidedbecause though there is an enemy, the enemy is not exercised but controlled so that its disposition and moves should force the forcebeing exercised with problems of the director's choosing. Whereas, a two-sided exercise on the other hand, has the two forces opposing each other equally exercised. There is therefore no 'controlled enemy'. Each side is given fullliberty to plan against the other, and to execute the plan.
The restriction of liberty of a person subject to service Law, who is alleged to have committed an offence against that law, from leaving theprecincts of a camp, barracks or area without permission.

The stocks of materiel required for day-to-daymaintenance based on the frequency of delivery into the operational theatre and the time taken to distribute them within the theatre. They include:a.First Line Stocks.These cover all expendable materiel held by units but exclude Combat reserves. They are controlled by the unit commander.b.Second Line Stocks.Stocks held immediately behind first line (e.g., stocks held by ST Coys and OFP) scaled to support first line stocks. Second line units do not normally hold combat reserves.Second line stocks are controlled by formation HQ.c.Other stocks.Stocks dispersed in materiel holding units and installations in or behind the combat zone (CZ).

Orders issued in writing or given orally by acommander to subordinate commanders, concerning operation. It contains the mission and how to accomplish it. The sequence and format arestandardized and subject to certain mandatory rules to guard against forgetfulness and aid clarity. Op Os should be as clear and brief as possible,unambiguous and absolutely accurate in matters of detail.

OOTW is used to describe those military actions that fall short of general or regional war. It covers: counter terrorism (CT), counter insurgency (COIN), peacekeeping, peace support operations (PSO),non-combatant evacuation operations (NEO)observer missions and other related military activity.

Operational art involves the control and direction of large forces (usually armies/army group) in combat activities within a single, discrete theatre of combat. It is the theory and practice of planning, preparingand conducting campaigns to accomplish operational and strategic objectives or end state.

In MAW, operations are organised within a framework of deep, close and rear operations for the purpose of carrying out the core functions, (find, fix, strike and exploit).a.Deep Operation.Deep Operation is usually conducted at long range over a protracted time scale against the enemy's forces and resources not currently engaged in close battle. The purpose is to find and fix the enemy to keep him from his objectives and restrict his freedom of action thereby creating conditions for close operation.b.Close Operation.Close Operation is usually at short range and in an immediate time scale. Its purpose is to strike the enemy to eliminate the discreet part of his combat power.c.Rear Operation.Rear Operation increases overall depth of operation and provide the resources to sustain the tempo of the combat operation. It ensures freedom of action and manoeuvre of uncommitted forces.

Because operations cannot be conductedcontinuously, there may be a need for periodic pauses, while retaining the initiative in other ways. Operational pauses may be needed when anoperation has temporarily reached the end of its sustainability; this could be because the troops involved are exhausted, or terrain and climate compel a halt, or the character of the campaign has changed (for instance a pursuit meets a hardening defence) or due to a combination of these factors.

The aim of operational security is toprovide a military operation with an additional degree of security, using active or passive means, to ensure that knowledge offriendly dispositions,capabilities, intentions and vulnerabilities are denied to the enemy.

In CRW operations in depth are designed to locate,disrupt and destroy hard core insurgents outside controlled areas, with a view to relieving a better chance of success. Operations in depth may be launched from temporary bases established in the area of operations, or they may take the form of an ''in and out'' operations launched direct from a main or forward operation base.

In order to maintain the flexibility and fluidity of landoperations and allow tempo to be varied, three major operations of war are recognised:offensive, defensiveandStability operations.a.Offensive Operation.Offensive Operation is the decisive operation of war. The purpose is to defeat the enemy by imposing our will on him by the application of focused violence, not only on the enemy's forward elements but throughout his depth. Examples are:(1) Attack.(2) Raid.(3) Exploitation.(4) Pursuit.(5) Feint.(6) Demonstration.(7) Reconnaissance in Force.(8) Ambush.(9) Break out.b.Defensive Operation.The usual purpose of a defensiveoperation is to defeat or deter a threat in order to provide the rightcircumstances for offensive action. Examples of DefensiveOperations are:(1) Defence.(2) Delaying operation. 'See'.c.Stability Operations.Some forms of stability operations are:(1) Security & Control.(2) Initial Restoration of Essential Services & Utilities.(3) Interim Governance Tasks.(4) Military Support to Security.(5) Sector Reform.

The Operations Officer is the battlegroup commander's principal operations staff officer. He is the commander's main assistant in coordinating and planning the battle and is also the battlegroup NBC advisor.

The seizure of a bridge or minefield lane by advancing with unexpected speed or from an unexpected direction or by the use of coup de main forces introduced by helicopter. Also known as 'bounced' crossings.
A list of units and lower formations which makeup a formation. It is set out so as to show the chain of command. Units and formations in direct support or in support are clearly shown as such.

Orders are defined as 'a communication, written, oral or by signal, which conveys instructions from a superior to a subordinate'. Orders are usedin all spheres of military activities and at all levels of command. They include sufficiently detailed direction to subordinates (in the form of missions and/ortasks) so that they can achieve specific activity, such as the deployment and employment of troops.
A group assembled to receive orders.

An ordnance corps' unit allocated on a scaleof one per brigade. It is fully mobile and holds:a. Stocks of fast moving items of MT and technical spares for the maintenance and repair of vehicles, weapons, radios and other major equipment in units.b. A stock of fast moving items of general store.c. A very limited scale of controlled stores such as personal weapons and radios sets.

Ordnance stores cover:a. Technical stores including spares, assemblies, and complete technical equipment such as guns, radios and generating sets.b. Mechanical transport stores including spares and assemblies for all vehicles.c. Clothing Items.d. General stores including tent age and camp equipment.e. Stationery including office machinery.
An organisation is defined as 'two or more people working together in a co-ordinated manner so as to achieve group result'.
Overlay Orders are the combination of written and graphic instructions on one trace containing enough information for a commander to carry out his specified tasks.
Firing across the frontage of mutually supportingSubunits.
To cover the frontage of forward elements from behind and retain the capability to deal with enemy therein, through direct fire.
The time of drop of the first stick of the main force in an airborne operation.

Military operations designed to clear an area ofimmediate insurgent influence and re-establish civil control. Military forces will continue to provide security until Para-military and police forces can acceptresponsibility.
Forces or group which are distinct from the regulararmed forces of any country but resemble them in organization and training and in the mission they undertake.
Parapet is aprotective wall of earth;a bank of soil, rubble, or sandbags piled up along the edge of a military trench for protection from enemy fire.
Personnel qualified to jump out of airborne aircraft using parachutes.

In the teaching of 'Law of War', a party to a conflict is a State that is formally or in fact involved in hostilities against one or more State. Such a State and its armed forces is a ''belligerent''.

In the teaching of 'Law of War', a party to a treaty is a State that is bound by the international treaties it has accepted (by ''ratification'' or ''accession''). a ''Party'' to the said treaty. A State can, when accepting atreaty, make national interpretation and/or reservations.
A pass is a road or track over a mountain range.
The actual time between the moment the leading vehicle of a column or element passes a given point and the moment when the last vehicle passes the same point.
When different troops are used for each phase of anoperation, they will often pass through secure areas held by other troops at the beginning of their assault. This is known as the passage of lines.

A specifically designated place where units will passthrough one another either in advance or withdrawal. It is located where the commander desires subordinate units physically to execute a passage oflines.
Any device which does not radiate to gaininformation and is therefore secure.
A secret word or distinctive sound used to reply to achallenge.

A team trained to recce, locate and secure DZs and LZs, provide navigational assistance to guide aircraft to DZs and LZs, and help in control within the LZ/DZ. They are introduced in a clandestine manner (e.g.,through free fall) to avoid loss of surprise.
A detachment of ground, sea, or air forces sent out for the purpose of gathering information or carrying out a destructive, harassing, mopping up, orsecurity mission.
Temporary bases to provide a comparatively secure area in which patrols can rest and recuperate, and from which patrol activities can be launched.

An officer who is responsible for the detailed organization and coordination of patrols. At brigade level this should be the SO3 G3 (Ops) and at BG HQ level the Ops Officer. The patrol master is responsible for:a. Keeping all patrol reports for reference.b. Maintaining a patrol situation map showing exact positions of own troops, minefields, pre-planned DFs, information from earlier patrols, previous and proposed patrol routes.c. Passing briefing information at Sub-Para b above, plus air photographs and maps to patrol briefing officers.d. Drawing up an accurate description of each patrol task to avoid duplication.e. Adjusting patrol timings and routes to avoid repetition and clashes.
The weight of passengers and/or cargo.
The capacity of an aircraft expressed in weight available to the user.
Peace building is an action to identify and supportstructures which will tend to strengthen and solidify peace; or avoid a relapseinto conflict.

Peace Enforcement is the use of coercive operationswhen the belligerent parties may not consent to intervention. They are conducted under Chapter VII of the UN Charter, and designed to maintain, restore or enforce the terms specified in the mandate.
Authorised establishment of units and formations inpeace time. This may be beefed up in war to meet a 'war establishment'.

PKO are conducted under Chapter VI of the UN Charter. They are undertaken with the consent of all major parties to the conflict, to monitor and control implementation of a peace agreement in order to promote security and sustain life in area of potential or actual conflict.

PSOs are multi-functional operations involving military forces, civil police, non-governmental organisations and diplomatic humanitarian agencies. They are designed to achieve humanitarian goals orlong-termpeace settlements, and are conducted impartially in support of a UN or a regional body mandate.
Diplomatic action to bring hostile parties to a negotiating agreement, through such peaceful as those foreseen in Chapter VI of the UN Charter.

'Perfidy'' consists of committing a hostile act under the cover of a legal protection. The following acts are examples of perfidy:a. To pretend an intent to negotiate under a flag of truce.b. To pretend surrender.c. To pretend being incapacitated by wounds or sickness.d. To pretend being a civilian or non-combatant.e. To pretend having protected status by the use of flags, emblems or uniforms of the United Nations or of neutral States.

A tank position whereby the gunner can see over a crest through his periscope. It is a variation of turret down.The tank will have to move before targetengagement.The position provides complete protection as only periscope is visible from the front.

Personnel security covers the risk to individuals fromsubversion and terrorism, and includes controls to limit movement (curfews, out-of-bounds areas and guards) and to prevent contact between force personnel and potential enemy sympathizers.
In land operations, a form of offensive which seeks to break through the enemy's defence and disrupt the defensive system.
The progressive stages of, e.g., an assault an advance, etc.
A line utilized for control and coordination of militaryoperations, usually a terrain feature extending across the zone of action.

The internationally agreed phonetic alphabet is asfollows:A - AlphaB - BravoC - CharlieD - DeltaE - EchoG - GolfH - HotelI - IndiaJ - JulietK - KiloL - LimaM - MikeN - NovemberO - OscarP - PapaQ - QuebecR - RomeoS - SierraT - TangoU - UniformV - VictorW - WhiskeyX - X-rayY - YankeeZ - Zulu

Physical security covers the physical barriers (locks,walls, wire and fields of fire) to be created to deny access to classified or sensitive documents, equipment, military bases and sensitive areas, and todefeat/prevent physical attack.
A suitable area from where troop lift helicopters pick up troops.

Picketing is the means of securing a road or track bydominating the route for a limited period to allow the safe passage of a convoy. It is expensive in manpower and time, and should only be carried outwhen there is a grave threat of ambush, and when other methods of protecting the route are impracticable.
Pillage is to plunder place or steal possessions using force, especially during a war.

Radio logs are maintained on all radio nets wheneverpracticable; to maintain a complete and continuous record of all transmittedand received messages and information concerning the radio net. The logshould be written legibly in the operator's own hand.
A group of stations working on the same frequency for the purpose of communicating with each other. All nets fall into one of thefollowing three categories:

Radio logs are maintained on all radio nets wheneverpracticable; to maintain a complete and continuous record of all transmitted and received messages and information concerning the radio net. The logshould be written legibly in the operator's own hand.

A group of stations working on the same frequency for the purpose of communicating with each other. All nets fall into one of the following three categories:a.Simple Net.This is a radio net consisting of a control station and two or more substations operating together on a common frequency for the purpose of communicating with one another.b.Combined Net.A combined net is one where two or more nets which normally operate separately are joined together, on a common frequency so that all stations can communicate directly with one another.When a combined net is formed, the former Control(s) of the junior net(s) and their substations assume the role of substations subordinate to the senior net's Control.c.Rebroadcast Net.A Rebroadcast Net is a radio net using radio rebroadcast (RRB) to extend the geographical area of a net, or to join together two or more individual nets.
Apoint-to-pointradio system of communication providing voice (telephone), telegraph (tele printer), data and FAX facilities.

All radio nets consist of two types of radio station known as;Control Station andsubstations.a.Control Station.Control Station is one of the stations on a radio net serving the senior headquarters or location. Control has theauthority and the responsibility for controlling communications, the flow of message traffic and enforcing radio discipline.b.Substations.Substations are all other stations on a radio net. They are subordinate to, and must obey orders from Control Station.

Radio silence can be defined as a passive measure for defence against the ESM process. It is an ordered state and is part of the counter surveillance measures. No radios are permitted to transmit exceptwhen using authorised 'break' procedures.
A non-voice communication by telegraph usingmorse.

An operation, usually on a small scale, involving a swift penetration of hostile territory to secure information, confuse the enemy, or destroy hisinstallations. It ends with a planned withdrawal upon completion of the assigned mission.
The laying of mines without regard to pattern.
Range card is a card containing 6 or 8 concentric circles, showing distances of objects in metres to be used in periods of poor visibility.
Primarily includes food (fresh or composite) and water but may also cover water purification chemicals, disinfectants and solid fuel cookers.
A line drawn from the position of the observer, to represent the direction of an object.

Real estate is an area allocated to a unit or formation, though not always for its exclusive use, for tactical and administrative purposes. Allocation is often done in multiples of square kilometres and is controlled bythe appropriate HQ. Where more than one user is allocated a particular area, the superior HQ will establish a status of command between the users and the responsibilities that go with the relationship. One unit will be nominated as the Priority 1 user (in effect the landlord), the remaining users (the lodgers) willnormally be TACON to the landlord. It is the responsibility of Brigade HQ to ensure that the real estate allocated to a particular unit is appropriate to the size and role and/or mission of that unit. Unless stated otherwise, Battlegroups will be the Priority 1 users of all real estate within their operational boundaries.
Measures taken before, during and after the event tominimize the effects of airborne attack, sabotage, infiltration, guerrilla action, psychological or propaganda warfare.

An area rear of the DAA created when a division is operating independently without the backingof higher formation HQ. A rear DAA is formed in order to:a. Provide logistic links between units in the divisional area and the static central or base units supporting the operation.b. Avoid concentrating a large number of logistic units in the DAA.c. Overcome the lack of unit transport as the majority of units in the rear DAA will require NACST third line transport to move.
An area to which tanks go when released by the localcommander from the forward rally and in which full replenishment and maintenance takes place.

An operation where a force effecting amovement to the rear passes through the sector of a unit occupying adefensive position. A rearward passage of lines may be conducted:a. As part of a delaying operation.b. As a means of changing the type of force facing the enemy.c. When terrain can be abandoned.d. As a means of relieving a force unable to continue with its mission.e. As part of a withdrawal operation.

Use of open, organized, and armed resistance in which the inhabitants of an area seek to obtain autonomy or independence (as distinguished from making an attempt to alter or overthrow the centralgovernment).
The process whereby materiel declared worn or scrap is restored to a condition which renders it fit for further use.

A mission undertaken to obtain, by visual observation or other detection methods, information about the activities and resources of an enemy or potential enemy, or to secure data concerning the meteorological, hydrographic, or geographic characteristics of a particular area.
A method of reconnaissance in which fire isplaced on a suspected enemy position to cause the enemy to disclose hispresence by movement or return of fire.
An offensive operation designed to discoverand/or test the enemy's strength or to obtain other information.
For ground forces, a patrol used to gain tacticalinformation preferably without the knowledge of the enemy.
Reconnaissance, Intelligence, Surveillance and Target Acquisition(RISTA)..

RISTA is a structure within which information collected through systematic observation is integrated with that collected from specific missions and processed in order to meet the commander's intelligence requirements. It also permits the detection, identification and location of targets in sufficient detail and in good time to allow successful engagement by offensive strike assets.

The expansion of force structures and infra-structurebeyond existing levels, including the raising of new units and formations and the expansion of industrial capacity to support the procurement of equipmentand stocks.

The term recovery covers a wide range of tasks for which EME is responsible. These extend from the extrication under fire of an immobilized AFV, to clearing equipment casualties from the battlefield to a maintenance point after the battle has moved on.
The utilisation of resources after Transfer of Authority (TOA) necessary for the fulfilment of the commander's combat missions.
A re-entrant occurs where the hillside is curved inwardstowards the main features; it is always found between two salients.

Persons who, because of real or imagined danger, move on their own volition, spontaneously or in violation of a stay-put policy, irrespective of whether they move within their own country (nationalrefugees) or across international boundaries (international refugees).
The timely activation, in full or in part, of existing forcestructures and infrastructure, including the restoration of manning, equipment and stocks to war levels.
The medical subunit that provides first line medical cover to the unit to which it is attached. It is usually attached to units of battalion and equivalent status.

The RSO is responsible for all communications matters and is also one of the watch-keepers. He conducts the recce of potential main locations and, during moves, deploys with Step- Up. He is responsible for the routine administration and support of battlegroup HQ.

Regrouping is the changing of a force from one command to another and it should be kept to minimum. Nevertheless, any force beingregrouped must know:a. Under whose command it will be.b. Command relationship.c. Outline of future task d. Time command changes.e. RV or hide areas to which it is to move (incl routes).f. Method of receiving detailed Os.g. Method of receiving new communications instructions.h. New arrangements for CSS.

Rehabilitation is essentially the restoration of combat power in order to prepare a unit or formation for re-employment. It is the process usually in a relatively quiet area, of units or individuals recently withdrawnfrom combat or arduous duty, during which units recondition equipment and are rested, furnished special facilities, filled up with replacements, issuedreplacement supplies and equipment, given training and generally made ready for employment in future operations.
Rehearsal is the act or process of practising an action in preparation for the actual conduct of that activity.

In artillery usage, a tactical mission in which one artillery unit augments the fire of another artillery unit. This task is a guarantee of fire though an artillery unit can only reinforce another artillery unit and not an allarms formation.
The replacement of manpower in war mainly due tocasualties sustained.
A request for reinforcement by aformation, unit or subunit sent on a format given in SOPs.

When communications between any two stations fail,messages between them may be sent through a third station which is incommunications with both of them; this third station is known as the 'relaystation'.

In road movements, a well-defined point on a route atwhich the elements composing a column return under the authority of their respective commanders, each one of these elements continuing its movement towards its own appropriate destination.
The ability of an item to perform a required function under stated conditions for a specified period of time.

A combat operation in which by direction of higher authority, allor part of a unit is replace in a combat area by another unit. The incoming unitcontinue the operation. Relief in line is normally conducted in an offensiveoperation.

An operation in which, by direction of higher authority, all orpart of a unit is replaced in an area by the incoming unit. The responsibilities ofthe replaced elements for the mission and the assigned zone of operationsare transferred to the incoming unit. Relief in place is normally conducted indefensive operations and might occur in any of the following circumstances:a.When the existing force is depleted or exhausted and needs to bereplaced.b.When troops of one capability or role need to be replaced bytroops of a different role.c.For routine rotation of troops.

A mine not directly emplaced, but delivered by artillery, missile, rocket, mortar, or similar means, or dropped from an aircraft. A ground launched mine with a range of less than 500m is notconsidered to be an RDM.
A pre-arranged meeting at a given time and locationfrom which to begin an action or phase of an operation, or to which to returnafter an operation.
The internal distribution of personnel and equipment in a formation or unit to render it battle worthy again, albeit at a reduced size. Formation/unit integrity remains.

The process whereby unfit complete equipment''™s and assemblies are moved from unit to, and through, the repair organisation and fit items returned to unit or stock. It may encompass a forward loop betweenthe units and their supporting field workshop, and a rearward loop from the field force to the base support organisation. It embraces the functions of recovery, evacuation, repair, materiel resource planning and supply management.
Technical operation to restore operational functions to an equipment or repairable damaged parts by adjustment, manufacture or the replacementof defective components.
Re-fill or restock to a predetermined level or quantity.

Replenishment in operation is of 2 types; routine and battle.a.Routine Replenishment.Routine replenishment will take place each night, with the day's expenditure being replaced. Standard loads will be passed forward automatically.b.Battle Replenishment.Battle replenishment will be instituted when expenditure is greater than routine replenishment capacity. Wheninstituted, loads will be passed forward on demand at any time of day or night.

In land warfare, Report Line is an easily recognizable feature like road, railway, stream or line of high ground. It need not be of tactical important but is used by advancing troops to report progress. It is nicknamed and preferably at right angle to the axis.
Resection is one of the methods of finding own position on the map by observing the bearing of or drawing lines from at least two previously fixed or known points.

An uncommitted and specifically earmarked reaction force to be employed in an emergency as operational exigencies dictate, e.g. to counterattack a lost position in the defence or to react to a sudden enemythreat from an unexpected direction.

A target for demolition, the destruction of which must be controlled at a specific level of command because it plays a vital part in the tactical or strategic plan, or because of the importance of the structure itself, or because the demolition may be executed in the face of the enemy.

Those stocks of materiel which are held to insure againstemergency, unexpected increases in usage and delays and loses in transit.The total reserve in a theatre consists of:a.Combat reserves held by units and installations in or behind the CZ.b.Other theatre reserve held by units and installations in the Comm Z.

Resilience is the term used to describe activities andstructures that ensure the Government can continue to function and deliver essential public services in time of crisis, including terrorist attack.
One who actively resists enemy's attempt of indoctrinating him.

A line established between converging friendly forces (one or both may be moving) that prohibits all fire support across the line without co-ordination with the affected force. The RFL is established by the commanders of both forces on identifiable terrain ''“ usually closer to the stationary force.
The act of replenishing stocks in order to maintain required levels of supply.
A tactical task to occupy and hold a terrain feature to ensure it is free of enemy occupation or use.
A retirement is a movement away from the enemy by a force out of contact and it is administrative in nature.
An open expression of disaffection by subjects with the established government or its policies.

An effort by dissidents to overthrow an establishedgovernment or administration and replace it with one of their choosing. The revolutions may accomplish their aim without necessarily resorting to the useof arms.

A tumultuous disturbance of the peace by three or more persons who are assembled together without lawful authority and with intention of mutuallyhelping one another, by force if necessary, against any opposition.
Road blocks and check points are a meansof controlling movement on roads, tracks and footpaths.

A rolling attack is two or more successive attacks byaviation normally co-ordinated by the battlegroup. A rolling attack will probably require fire teams to relay through a Forward Arming and Refuelling Point (FARP) to resupply.

Reconnaissance to obtain detailed information of a specified route and all adjacent terrain from which the enemy could influence movement along that route. Route recce may also be to obtain information ofan enemy force moving generally along a specific route, or to locate sites for the construction of hasty obstacles to impede enemy's movement.

Rover is a man portable receive-only terminal that provides the capability to receive real time sensor data from suitably equipped airborne platforms. This data is in the form of a real motion video, if correctly used, 'Rover' can enhance the prosecution of CAS by reducing the risk of fratricide and reducing the engagement cycle time.

ROE define the degree and manner in which force may be applied and are designed to ensure that such application of force is carefully controlled; ROE limit the use of force in such a way that it will be used only in a manner consistent with the overall military objective. For example, units deployed on a peacekeeping mission may be restricted to theuse of force only when acting in self-defence of themselves and other peacekeeping troops.
To create a gap in enemy defensive positions quickly.
Sabot is a sleeve placed around a projectile to support it, so that it can be fired from a weapon with a large bore e.g. eagle tank. The sabot drops away shortly after the projectile is fired.
Any action short of a normal military operation, or an omission, which involves physical damage or tempering with facilities not in the nationalinterest.
A piece of high ground jutting out from a main feature or range of hills.
An operation consisting of taking one or more sub-assemblies or spare parts from unrepairable equipment or supplies (salvage is permanentcannibalisation).
Stands for Slidex, Callsign, Address Group, Net Identification Sign and Telephone Exchange List.
A soldier (or person) posted ahead or to the flanks of a small body of troops to provide local early warning of the enemy. Scouts are employed at subunit and below levels.
Screens are covering troops deployed to observe, identify andreport on en movement and other information. They only fight inself-protection.
The CSS organic to a brigade or a division.

That position, apart from the primary position, fromwhere the primary arc of another weapon or an enemy approach other than the main approach may be covered. The alternative secondary position isone from where the secondary position tasks may still be carried out when the secondary position is left.
An area designated by boundaries within which a unit operates, and for which it is responsible.

In an operational context, to gain possession of a position or terrain feature, with or without force, and to make such disposition as willprevent, as far as possible, its destruction or loss by enemy action.
Protection against unauthorised disclosure (e.g., of information) and admittance to (e.g. an installation) or interference of any kind.

The category of grade given to the defence ofinformation contained in a document. It indicates the degrees of danger to national (or allied) security that would result from its unauthorized disclosureand the protection to be given to guard against such a disclosure. The four security classifications are:a.Top secret.Security classification grading given toinformation and material, the unauthorized disclosure of which would cause exceptionally grave damage to the nation. This is the highest security classification in the NA.b.Secret.Security classification grading given to information and material, the unauthorized disclosure of which would causeserious injury to the interest of the nation.c.Confidential.Security classification grading given to information and materials the unauthorized disclosure of which would be prejudicial to the interest of the nation.d.Restricted.Security classification grading indicating that the unauthorized disclosure of the informationand/or material so graded would be undesirable to the interest of the nation.
All indigenous and allied police, military and Para-military forces used by a government to maintain law and order.
Gain possession of a position or terrain, normally by force.

Seizing the initiative means having the power to makethe enemy react to your agenda. To seize and retain the initiative requires a constant effort to force the enemy to conform to your operational purpose andtempo whilst retaining freedom of action. To achieve this, battlegroup commanders must be prepared to act independently within the framework ofthe higher commander's intent.
In operational art, sequencing is the arrangement of events within a campaign in the order most likely to achieve the elimination of the enemy's centre of gravity.

Commanded letters are formal lettersssued by the Ministry of Defence in the name of the Defence Council, or one of the Service Councils or Boards and reserved for statements of major policy, directives and letters of special character.They are normally signed by Assistant Secretaries or aboveaccording to the nature and importance of the subject. There is no laid down format.

These are letter used by the Ministry of Defence for correspondence at a level between Commanded Letters and Routine Letters. Staff officers may be authorized to sign such letters at the discretion of directors or heads of divisions.

Routine letters are normal form of correspondences within and between the services. A routine lettermay be written by a formation or unit to any other formation or unit or to the Ministry of Defence, or by an individual member of the serviceson a personal subject.

A formal letter is a service letter addressedonly to a senior or equal on occasions such as the following:(1) In reply to a letter of praise or blame.(2) When making a submission of an exceptional nature or forwarding a non-routine report to higher authority.(3) In arranging ceremonial matters with outside authorities.
A DO Letter allows an informal and more personal approach to service or civil addressees.

A memo is a form of internal correspondence on local matters at all levels and within departments,headquarters or units. It is designed to save time and is normally written in manuscript though a printed memorandum form may be used. Abbreviations may be used throughout.

Loose minutes are used extensively within theMOD, headquarters and Service units when it is nec to disseminate information but inappropriate or inconvenient to circulate a file. Whatever form a loose or an internal minute may take, it should still befiled in the same way as all other correspondences but should never be distributed outside the originating headquarters or unit.
A comprehensive report of hostile shelling. The format is contained in SOPs. Similar reports are made for hostile mortaring, bombing and jamming (MORTREP, BOMREP and JAMREPrespectively),
Shelter is that part of the battle trench which provides overhead protection.

A psychological effect that leads to low morale and loss of the will to fight, produced, for example, by the bold employment of amour, exploiting all four characteristics of firepower, protection, mobility andflexibility.

Courier service provided by the Corps ofSignals using motorcycles, vehicles or even aircraft. The SDS has an important role to play especially when radio silence has been imposed. SDSpersonnel also provide postal facilities.
The analyzed information derived from Electronic Support Measures (ESM). SIGINT is divided into:
C O M I N T i s derived from the analysis of information gained from intercepting enemy communications.

ELINT is used to obtain technical data on enemy data processing command and control systems, telemetry links and control and guidance techniques usedfor individual weapon systems, e.g., radio frequency, IR, TV or laser, and the ECCM measures employed.
A chart showing the state of comm on a net, i.e., how the stations read each other.

Night attack with planned fire support on call, but following the serials on the timed programme silently. The main aim is to achieve surprise. Invariably though, every silent attack must turn to a noisy one atsome stage of the attack. See Noisy Attack.
Simulated fire equipment are realistic trainingaids for field exercises with troops. They duplicate the flash and bang effects of weapons.
Simultaneity is the overloading of an enemy commander by attacking or threatening him in so many ways at once that he cannot concentrate on any one, nor establish priorities between them.
A single call is a type of call made by any station to any other single station on the net.

In conducting IPB, he Situation Overlay combines aDoctrinal Overlay with the BAE. It shows how the threat COAs is constraint by the terrain and other characteristics of the battlefield environment. TheSituation Overlays also shows, by means of Time Lines how the effect of terrain may cause the units to travel at different speeds.

A report covering the operational situation of aformation or unit over a specified period. It includes both own and enemy information and distributed to superior and flanking formations/units foractions and subordinate formations/units for information.
Exercise on a reduce scale designed to train commander and staff officers, e.g., indoor telephone battles.

A Procedure for encoding words and phrases at all levels of command, for purposes of security. All messages which may be of value to the enemy, sent over unsecured net radio and on which action may not be taken within the next thirty minutes, must be encoded inSlidex .

'Slow Go'' areas are grounds over which manoeuvre of a deployed force is only considered possible at a reduced speed or with the deployment of additional asset. It must be assessed according to the type offorce, for example armour, wheeled and dismounted forces have different requirements and constraints.

Use of smoke to blind enemy observation (and to prevent observed fire by his artillery and aimed fire by the small arms, tank and antitank weapons), to screen the movement of own troops and for deception.

Techniques of movement by a mechanized, recce or tank platoon on a road, route or other circumstances where the platoon is unable to advance on a wider front. The movement is in line ahead formation (singlefile) and a leading vehicle must never be out of sight of its supporting (following) vehicle.
An operation to capture a wanted person. It is basedon information concerning the precise whereabouts of the wanted person and must be carefully planned, rehearsed and aimed to achieve surprise.
A locating device with the help of which hostile guns and mortars can be located and own weapons can be ranged to enemy guns by sound adjustment.
Socio-Economic Factors include anything which constrains the action of friendly forces, e.g. to avoid civilian casualties or prevent the destruction of important facilities.
A source is a person from whom, or a thing fromwhich, information can be obtained. An agency is an organisation or individual engaged in collecting and processing information.

Special Forces are strategic troops who are selected,trained, equipped and organised to special levels and are usually employed in pursuit of national objectives. They operate in support of conventionalforces or independently. e.g., airborne forces.
A tactical manoeuvre employed to impair seriously ahostile attack while the enemy is in the process of forming up or assembling for an attack.
A check on a single aspect of a logistic requirement, e.g., transport for a dumping programme.

Any officer working in a HQ excluding the commander. The duty of the staff in a nutshell is to:a. Assist the commander in the function of command.b. Help both the fighting troops and the service in carrying out their tasks.

Table which contains in a readily accessible form, information about various units that a staff officer may require in carrying out his duties. This information,based on unit returns or their establishment may be used for such purpose like:a. Road movement.b. Preparation of landing tablec. Preparation of air loading tabled. Calculations for the amount of combat supplies needed.

An area located between the mounting area and theobjective area through which all or part of the forces pass after mounting, for the purpose of refuelling, regrouping, training, inspection and distribution oftroops and materiel.

Stand to is a procedure adopted where every man takes up position in his fire trench with his weapon ready for immediate use when enemy in suspected to be in the vicinity or when enemy is likely to attack aposition. As a routine stand to is held at dawn and dusk or when sizeable body of troops has either joined in or gone out.

Laid down tactical and administrative drills, procedures and standing orders designed to save time and prevent mistake in the fields. It makes of smooth functioning of the HQ, formation of unit concerned. Also called Standard Operating Procedures.

The process of developing concepts, doctrines,procedures and designs to achieve and maintain the most effective levels of compatibility, interoperability,inter-changeability and commonality in the fields of operations, administration and materiel.

Line which assaulting troops cross at H-Hour. Normally the forward edge of the FUP (see) must be easily recognizable and preferably square to the objective.The SL also help to align attacking troops with the objective.
A designated point on the ground expressed as a6-figure grid reference from where a given activity commences.
The state of a demolition target in whichcharges are in place. The firing circuit may be in place, but the detonators are not installed and the means of firing are not connected.
The state of a demolition target in which the demolition charges are in place, the firing and priming circuits are installed and complete, ready for immediate firing.

The states of command describe the status of formations or units relative to another unit or formation. They are concerned primarily with the ability of the receiving formation to assign an independent mission, to reorganise the formation to suit its purpose or to direct specific tasks within an agreed mission. The various states of command include:
a. Full Command (Full Comd). Full Comd is the military authority and responsibility of a superior officer to issue orders to subordinates. It covers every aspect of military operations and administration.
b. Operational Command (OPCOM). OPCOM is the authority granted to a commander to assign missions or tasks to subordinate commanders, to deploy units, to re-assign forces and to retain or delegate operational and/or tactical control as may be deemed necessary. It does not xc include responsibility for administration or logistics.
c. Operational Control (OPCON). OPCON is the authority delegated to a commander to direct forces assigned so that the commander may accomplish specific missions or tasks which are usually limited by function, time or location; to deploy units concerned, and to retain or assign tactical control of those units. It does not include authority to assign separate employment of components of the units concerned neither does it include administration or logistic control.
d. Tactical Command (TACOM). TACOM is the authority delegated to a commander to assign tasks to forces under his command for the accomplishment of the mission assigned by higher authority.
e. Tactical Control (TACON). TACON is the detailed and usually local direction and control of movement and manoeuvre necessary to accomplish missions or tasks assigned. This includes the coordination of real estate.
f. Under Command Administration (UCADMIN). This implies complete transfer of administrative/logistic command i.e. all services and personnel matters. It includes responsibility for all G1 matters including medical and provost.
g. Under Command for Admin (With Caveats) (UCADMIN...). When the temporary nature of the command makes it unnecessary to effect a complete change of administrative command, a formation or
unit may be placed under command for certain specific matters, or for administration less certain administrative matters.
h. Under Command for Daily Maintenance (UCDM). This state of command leaves the original parent formation or unit HQ with full responsibility for all administration less daily maintenance. The commander responsible for daily maintenance is responsible only for daily replenishment of combat supplies, evacuation of casualties, the provision of common user supply items and the repair and recovery of equipment.
A generic term conveying the quantities of items of materiel held on charge, as opposed to materiel in use.

There are four types of stragglers:
a. Men who have genuinely lost their way and are attempting to rejoin their company group.
b. Men who, by reason of their mental and/or physical condition, cannot be held responsible for their actions.
c. Men running away through fear.
d. Men who, through no fault of their own, have become separated from their company group and are attempting to rejoin them.

a. Grand/National Strategy. The process of obilizing and directing in the most effective way all the resources of a nation including the armed forces to safeguard and promote its interests against those of its enemies, actual or potential. It is the application of national resources to achieve policy objectives.
b. Military Strategy. Military strategy is strictly concerned with the employment of military power during peace and in war to fulfil the aim of the grand strategy or foreign policy. In peacetime, it determines how military forces are deployed to deter war. In wartime, it involves producing the conditions under which tactical operations can take place and guides the employment of military forces in pursuit of victory.
See ''Core Functions of the Manoeuvrist Approach''.
Strong point is a heavily fortified position tied to a natural or reinforcing obstacle to create an anchor for the defence or to block a key piece of terrain.
Strong point in FIBUA is a section or a platoon post sited around a round intersection with fire positions in two or three different buildings with interlocking and mutually sp fire.
All other stations on a radio net apart from the control station. See 'Radio Station'.
A 3 letter group which identifies the subject matter of a message and provides delivery instructions for sig messages.
Action taken to undermine the military, economic, psychological, morale or political strength of a nation and the loyalty of the subjects.

The two methods of reducing evidence to writing are: Summary of Evidence and Abstracts of Evidence. Reducing evidence to writing may be necessary if for example, a CO investigating a case under certain circumstance, (like if the maximum punishment for the offence with which the accused is charged is death) before he submits the charge to higher authority, or hear the evidence himself.

A fire unit, normally the direct support battery, tasked with providing additional fire on a target already allotted a fire unit; hence the word 'superimposed.' The idea is to:
a. Ensure that an objective allotted a superimposed fire unit is not left unattended when the superimposed fire unit if lifted for other tasks.
b. Prevent the direct support battery sitting idle while awaiting an impromptu or on call target.

A detailed and comprehensive report which elaborates on intelligence collected over a period of time. Normally originated at divisional headquarters and above level with a controlled distribution. Preceded by the abbreviation SUPINTREP.
All materiel and items used in the equipment, support and maintenance of military forces.
The action of a force, or portion thereof, which aids, protects, complements, or sustains any other force.

A designated task in which a manoeuvre element moves to a position on the battlefield where it can engage the enemy by direct fire. The manoeuvre element does not attempt to manoeuvre to capture enemy forces or terrain.

An offensive operation carried out in conjunction with
a main attack and designed to achieve one or more of the following:
a. Deceive the enemy.
b. Destroy or pin down enemy forces which could interfere with the main attack.
c. Control ground whose occupation by the enemy will hinder the main attack.
d. Force the enemy to commit reserves prematurely or in an indecisive area.
Fire delivered by supporting units to assist or protect a unit in combat.

Surprise makes a major contribution to the breaking of the enemy's cohesion and his defeat. It is achieved by doing the unexpected and thereby creating opportunities and gaining the initiative from the enemy. Its effect can be enhanced through the use of speed, secrecy and deception. Security involves maintaining the initiative and enhancing freedom of action by limiting vulnerability to hostile activities and threats.

STAP enables battlegroup HQs to coordinate and control all available sensors in order to provide warning of the enemy's movement within their area of interest in sufficient time to react to it. The objective is to acquire the target that will be identified when it is in the location where your selected strike assets can most effectively be brought to bear.
The ability of a force to maintain the necessary level of combat power for the duration required to achieve the objective.

Sustainability Statement defines the level of CSS that is to be made available to a commander. A formal Sustainability Statement should always be prepared and be part of the overall planning for logistics when a force is to be deployed; it provides the basis for all subsequent CSS activities. It should at least include the following:
a. The expected duration of the deployment and the operation.
b. The quantity of ammunition that is required in theatre expressed in Days of Supply (DOS).
c. The quantity of all other materiel that is required in theatre.
d. The predicted casualty rate for men, either from battle or disease and non battle injuries; and equipment. e. Repair and recovery priorities by equipment and formation type.
The thorough search of an area to ensure that no enemy remains undetected in it or is able to escape. This action is more peculiar to CRW operations.

Synchronization is the focusing of resources and activities to produce maximum combat power at the decisive time and place. The product of effective synchronisation is maximum economy of force, with every resources being used when and where it will make the greatest contribution to success.

Synchronisation matrix links DSO with commander tactical plan by showing how the battle develops. It provides a useful graphical planning tool to assist the commander and his staff analysing own COA both in time and space in relation to the enemy's most likely COA. It should incorporate all offensive support, recce and manoeuvre. Production of the Synchronisation Matrix is a G3 function or the task of battlegroup 2IC at battle group level.
In operational art, synergy is a concept that relates to integrating and synchronizing operations.
Tactical air reconnaissance collects information on the enemy, weather and geographical features required for the planning and conduct of land operations.
The TAOR is the area in which commander intends his force to manoeuvre; and in which the threat forces that will affect, or be affected by these operations are also expected to deploy.

Exercise without troops aimed at teaching officers and SNCOs detailed application of tactical principles on the ground before the stage of an exercise with troops is reached. A TEWT must be framed to bring out certain definite lessons, e.g. the application of the principles of defence in a unit taking up a defensive position.

Tactical operations are operations at the tactical level
and they are as follows:
a. Reconnaissance and Security.
b. Offensive Operations.
c. Defensive Operations.
d. Delay Operations.
e. Transitional Operations.

Tactics is the techniques for using the combination of weapons and units for engaging and defeating an enemy in battle. It is the art of using resources to their best advantage, taking into account the composition of own force, the ground over which it has to operate, the strength and disposition of the enemy and his likely reaction to own moves. It is essentially the employment of units in combat.
Area of ground that is ''go and slow go'' to amour. The only ground not tankable is one over which it is physically impossible to move tanks even with engineer assistance.

An area where a tank unit or submit lies up for any length of time for a refit, maintenance and reorganization. It is usually well behind own Forward Defended Localities (FDLs) with concealment as the primary requirement. Also see Harbour.

An action, similar to the laying of ambushes, whereby
tanks are destroyed by small parties of infantry using own weapons. Tank hunting teams of two men (or even one suitably armed soldier) can be organized to stalk and destroy an unprotected tank in a defensive locality.

Target Acquisition is the process of collecting detailed
information about the location of enemy forces with sufficient accuracy to enable weapons systems to suppress or destroy those elements of the enemy selected as targets.
A TAI is an area where the commander can influence the battle by destroying, delaying or disrupting the enemy. TAIs can be Point TAIs, e.g. a bridge, or Area TAIs, e.g. a valley.
An easily recognised point on the ground (either natural or manmade) used to initiate, distribute and control fire.

TSS are criteria, applied to enemy activity (acquisitions and battlefield information), used in deciding whether the activity is a target. Targets meet accuracy and timeliness requirements for attack, while suspected targets must be confirmed before any attack.

This is the acquisition of targets and their subsequent attack. It is the process of selecting targets and matching appropriate response to them taking into account operational requirements and capabilities.
A temporary force task organized and equipped under one commander for a specific mission. The strength of a task force may lie between a reinforced battalion group and a division.

This is by cross-attaching sub-units (companies and squadrons) with the battlegroups based on the formation commander's estimate of the situation and subsequent plan for the impending operation. Task organisation should be constructed so that the battlegroup commander and his sub-unit commanders are able to fight their deep, close and rear battles as well as provide recce and security functions. Any subunit or battlegroup organization should comprise the ability to:
a. Find and fix.
b. Manoeuvre ''” strike.
c. Echelon ''” momentum
d. Reserve ''” uncommitted.
This is known as the 'rule' of four.

An indoor exercise aimed at teaching staff work and procedures which commanders and their staff will be expected to carry out in HQ in the field. Two levels of HQ can be exercised at the same time, e.g. a brigade HQ and its battalion group HQ or a divisional HQ and his brigade HQ. A telephone battle should provide a setting in which staff officers seek record, analyse and pass information, issue orders and instructions. The main communication channel is through use of telephones.

Tempo is the rate or rhythm of activity relative to the enemy, within tactical engagements and battles and between major operations. It incorporates the capacity of the force to effect the transition from one operation of war to another. Tempo consists of three elements; speed of decision, speed of execution and the speed of transition from one activity to another.
Termination is an essential component of strategy and operational art, whereby forces know when to terminate military operations and how to preserve achieved advantages.
Terrain is the combination of natural features, built-up areas and infrastructure.

The process of analysing the various terrain features, and categorising them as ''No Go, Slow Go and Go'' according to their predicted effect on the ability of the threat and friendly forces to manoeuvre over the ground.

A resort to violence by a dissident faction in order to intimidate and coerce people for political ends. This many manifest itself in sabotage and assassination by individuals or small groups, or in the form of ambushes or attacks on civilians or police by large bodies of terrorist. It can take place in either urban or rural areas.

In conducting IPB, TE consists of a series of discrete actions aimed at identifying the threat's overall capability, based on his doctrine. It is concerned with producing the Doctrinal Overlay. It is a 5-part process of:
a. Finding the threat ''“ Where is he.
b. Identify the threat ''“ Who is he and what are his assets and strength.
c. Assessing the threat ''“ What is his combat effectiveness because that will affect how it is likely to operate.
d. Predicting the threat's likely COAs.''“ What is he likely to do based on his doctrine i.e. how he usually operate if he is not constrained by the terrain.
e. Displaying the threat's likely COAs.''“ this is producing separate doctrinal overlays for each COA showing the likely effect on friendly forces.

In conducting IPB, TI combines Battlefield Area Evaluation (BAE) with Threat Evaluation (TE) to show how the threat COAs and the friendly forces ability to counter (i.e. own COAs) will be affected by the terrain. TI produces Situation Overlays and Event Overlays.
In conducting IPB, Time Line is a line on situation overlay which predicts the movement of threat forces at specific interval.
A concept whereby data from many sources is brought together to provide visibility of all assets thereby facilitating their control at the appropriate level of command.
Military police post established for traffic control, usually for specified periods, e.g. during a road move or in a river crossing operation.
Any towed vehicle that does not of itself process automotive power.
The term 'training' covers every aspect of military activity designed to increase a soldier's knowledge of his military skills, his self-confidence and his physical and mental fitness for war.

Transitional phases link the primary operations of war. They are as follows:
a. Advance to Contact. The advance to contact seeks to regain contact with the enemy under the most favourable conditions.
b. Meeting Engagement. A meeting engagement involves action between two moving forces.
c. Link-Up Operations. The aim of a link-up operation is to establish contact between two or more friendly units which may have the same or differing missions. They normally occur in enemy controlled territory.
d. Withdrawal. A withdrawal occurs when a force disengages from an enemy force in accordance with the will of its commander.
e. Relief Operations. Relief of troops in combat occurs when combat activities are taken over by one force from another. These are: Relief in place, Forward passage of lines and Rearward passage of lines.
Transmission Security is that component of COMSEC which includes all measures designed to protect our radio transmissions from enemy interception, analysis and deception.
The time that elapses between the auth for the transmission of a msg and its receipt of addresses.

a. First line. Unit transport which take over C Sups and other stores from second line transport at Dps.
b. Second line. ST transport for the maintenance of formations and units in the forwards areas.
c. Third line. ST transport under control or army/force/corps HQ.

The evaluation and classification of wounded for the purposes of treatment and evacuation. It consists of the immediate sorting of patients according to type and seriousness of injury, and likelihood of survival, and the establishment of priority for treatment and evacuation to assure medical care of the greatest benefit to the largest number. Triage is also the evaluation and classification of equipment for the purpose of repairs or evacuation.

That organization in an FTX whose tasks is to give
those being exercised a realistic impression of battle conditions, arbitrate between exercised troops and the controlled enemy when the former are attacked, assess damage and casualties and generally keep control informed of presents and future situations (see control organization).
A demolition target which has been prepared to receive charges, the charges being packaged and stored in a safe place.
Refers to information and material that bears no security classification and therefore does not require any authority to be disclosed.

A letter substitute code used to conceal temporarily the grid reference of a place referred to while carrying voice conversation within units.
It is not used with slide.
Ground, which alternatively rises and falls gently.

A unit officer trained as an assistant UEO (see), for the deplaning and unloading of his unit after an air move. He normally moves with the unit advance party and therefore cannot also act as the UEO.

An officer in the unit trained to be responsible for supervising the emplaning and loading of the unit into an aircraft. He is also responsible for:
a. Training the unit in all aspects of air movement including the use of helicopters.
b. Preparing and maintaining the unit air staff table.
c. Supervising the packaging and preparation of unit stores and equipment.
A unit equipment table shows the details of all equipment which is authorized for a unit to hold.
That element of First Line stocks that can be carried on unit transport.
A scaling of spares which are in frequent demand for repairs being carried out by unit or attached repair tradesmen.

Vehicles in the military are categorised as follows:
a. 'A' Vehicles. A' Vehicles are vehicles which are armoured and may be designed to carry offensive armament. This category includes specialist 'A' vehicles such as armoured engineer and
recovery vehicles and APCs.
b. 'B' Vehicles. 'B' Vehicles are unarmoured vehicles of all types including trailers; they are often referred to as soft skinned vehicles/
c. 'C' Vehicles. 'C' Vehicles are mobile items of earth moving equipment and all types of crawler, wheeled and truck mounted cranes and mechanical handling equipment.
d. 'D' Vehicles. 'D' Vehicles are amphibious vehicles designed for landing troops on beaches.
e. 'E' Vehicles. 'E' vehicles are basic B vehicles fitted with specialist equipment, e.g. Fitted for Radio (FFR) Land rover

The art of referring to the future by reference to past events of which the enemy has no knowledge of, e.g., ''send your sunray at the same time and place as yesterday.'' Veiled speech provides good security, provided it is not overdone.
The capability of an aircraft to take ''“ off and land vertically and to transfer to or from forward motion at heights required to clear surrounding obstacles.
Ground of such tactical importance that it must be retained or controlled for the success of the mission.

VPs are those points where it is particularly advantageous for the adversary to position an ambush, using bombs, bobby traps, or IEDs. Likely places are:
a. Culverts.
b. Bridges.
c. High banked stretches of road.
d. Routes dominated by high ground (possible firing points).
e. Junctions.
f. Buildings and walls near route.
g. Parked vehicles.
h. Prominent markers on routes (e.g. poles and road signs).
I. Location of previous attack.
j. Places where vehicles slow down (bends, potholes, debris, traffic calming areas).
k. Places where road narrows.

War crimes are violation of laws of war; they are crime committed during wartime that is in violation of international agreements concerning the conventions of war, e.g. the mistreatment of prisoners or genocide.

Stocks of materiel amassed in peacetime to meet the
increase in military requirements consequent upon an outbreak of war. War reserves are intended to provide the interim support to sustain operations until resupply can be effected.

These are rate that lay down the wastage for all items
of equipment vehicle and stores. They form the basis for provisioning for the army and for stocking the corps maintenance areas.

War gaming are simulations in which theories of warfare can be tested and refined without the need for actual hostilities. It can be anything from a computer driven analysis to a demonstration on a sand model or map. In the Commander's Estimate Process, war gaming is used to develop the detailed plan by comparing the COA determined by the commander with the most likely enemy COAs identified through the IPB process. It achieves this by helping the commander and his staff to visualise the flow of the operation.

That part of the missile, projectile and torpedo rocket or other ammunition which contains either the nuclear or thermonuclear system, high explosive system chemical or biological agents or insert material intended to inflict damage.

A warning order may be written, graphical or oral. It should initiate battle procedure. Warning orders should be issued as soon as possible and should not be delayed because all the information e.g. definitive tasks are not currently available. The warning order can be updated as information becomes available.
The line defining the lowest of a valley, occupied by a stream.

A ridge of land separating two drainage basins that is, the summit of land which water divides of flows in two different directions. A watershed normally includes the highest point of a chain of mountains or range of hills.

A WEZ is airspace of defined dimensions where the responsibility for engagement rests with a particular
weapon system. Some examples of WEZs include:
a. Fighter Engagement Zone (FEZ). For land based AD, a FEZ is airspace of defined dimensions where the responsibility for engagement of air threats normally rests with fighter aircraft.
b. Joint Engagement Zone (JEZ). A JEZ is airspace of specific dimensions where friendly SAMs and fighters are simultaneously employed
c. Short Range Air Defence Engagement Zone (SHORADEZ). ASHORADEZ is airspace of defined dimensions where the responsibility for engagement rests with short-range air defence weapons.

The earth is divided into 25 time zones, some ahead of GMT, and others behind. The Zone Time is that of a particular area relative to GMT. Each zone time is given a letter called the 'zone time suffix'. The zone time suffixes area as follow:

B + 2
C + 3
D + 4
E + 5
F + 6
G + 7

To get area with half hourly differences, two letters area are combined e.g. The zone time suffix of an area 41/2 hours ahead of GMT will be DE. Observe the letter J is missing in this arrangement.
